source.title: The twin peaks of learning neural networks
source.authors: E. Demyanenko; Christoph Feinauer; E. M. Malatesta; Luca Saglietti

record.tranche_reason: The study varies network capacity and measures test/generalization error, using a scaling sweep similar to the original double-descent tests, and reports results for new model settings.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own capacity sweeps, test/generalization errors, and BMD results. Epoch-wise double descent is mentioned in related work but not tested here; the adversarial-initialization experiment varies pretraining epochs but does not measure an ordinary test-error curve over training time. Figure-only curves are recorded as figure only. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own capacity sweeps of test/generalization error: replica theory and simulations for the random feature model, a two-layer MLP on MNIST, and a ResNet-18 width sweep on CIFAR-10 with label noise, as in 1912.02292. It also varies label noise, regularization and training-set size. Its main contribution, the Boolean Mean Dimension (BMD), is a sensitivity metric that co-peaks with test error. BMD is not itself a double-descent measure.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that BMD peaks sharply at the interpolation threshold together with the generalization-error peak, then decays to a task-dependent asymptote. The same holds across architectures and datasets, and regularization and label noise affect BMD as they affect double descent. They add that BMD needs no data, so it can flag overfitting, and that higher BMD goes with lower robustness and with adversarial initialization. In the optimally regularized RFM, BMD still peaks although test error is monotonic.
record.recipe_differences: Capacity is varied and test/generalization error is measured, as in the original model-wise double-descent approach; this study additionally measures BMD and uses its own model, data, and training settings.
record.method_sensitivity: Peak visibility depends on regularization and label noise. The peak's location and shape are also studied across model architecture, dataset, loss, and training-set size.

fits_no_version.finding: BMD peaks at the same capacity as the test/generalization-error peak across RFM (theory and MNIST), MLP and ResNet-18.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input-sensitivity (Boolean Mean Dimension) of the learned function peaks at the interpolation threshold together with the double-descent error peak.

fits_no_version.finding: Under per-α optimal regularization, RFM generalization error is monotonic while BMD still peaks then declines.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Function sensitivity can peak even when optimally regularized test error shows no double descent.

fits_no_version.finding: BMD curve shifts to larger width with more training samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The BMD peak tracks the sample-dependent interpolation threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Longer adversarial pretraining raises both test error and BMD.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial initialization jointly increases test error and sensitivity.

fits_no_version.finding: BMD anti-correlates with a pixel-flip robustness count, with minimum robustness at the BMD peak.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Networks near the interpolation threshold are least robust to random input flips.

record.problems: Several numerical curves are presented only as plots, with no exact peak values or locations stated. Some experiments use 5 repetitions, and the training-set-size result does not explicitly state that more data raises test error near the peak. The paper reports average curves and standard deviations but does not provide uncertainty values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-bearing results were omitted. Pixel-wise BMD contributions and self-averaging results were not extracted because they do not measure a listed claim version; the related robustness and adversarial-initialization findings are included under fits_no_version.

untested.parts: No test-error curve over ordinary training epochs. Epoch-wise double descent is only cited.
Sample-size curves are figure-only. The text says more data shifts the curve mostly downward and never states that more data raises error near the peak.
Epoch axis untested. No effective-complexity measure is defined or computed; only a qualitative statement that the peak follows the memorization capacity on the sample axis.
No sweep without label noise for the MLP or ResNet-18, and no larger architectures.

missing.what: Authors state optimizers' implicit regularization can strongly reduce the peak, and label noise was introduced to restore it in the presented figures.
missing.locator: Section 5.2, 'Position of the BMD peak' paragraph

missing.what: Text statement that more training samples shift the test-error peak to higher capacity, because more capacity is needed to memorize, while lowering error overall.
RFM generalization error vs. 1/α for αT=1 to 30 (λ=1e-4, MSE). The secondary N=D peak appears in BMD but 'is not present in the generalization'.

record.verdict_notes: Double-descent error curves here are mostly context for the BMD metric. The RFM theory largely reproduces Gerace et al. 2020, and several regularization statements restate prior work. The reader's V1 'challenges' label on r3 was wrong: optimal regularization removing the peak is V6's prediction. The BMD rows were moved out of V5 because BMD is a sensitivity metric, not an effective-complexity predictor of peak location.

versions.untested_parts: No broad sweep over every architecture or training regime; regularization changes the result.
No test-error curve over ordinary training epochs.
Training-set sizes are varied at fixed model/training setup, but the text does not state whether adding data raises test error near the peak; the relevant curves are figure-only.
Evidence is limited to the random feature model, a two-layer fully connected network, and ResNet-18; other model classes and the full classical U-shaped-to-double-descent account are not tested.
The study relates BMD and generalization peaks mainly along model capacity; it does not test a single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location along the epoch axis.
The study tests label-noise and regularization dependence, including one noisy-label secondary-peak setting. It does not establish that label noise or variance is the general cause of the peak.
No re-counting of complexity by an effective number of parameters or test of whether that yields an ordinary U-shaped curve.
